seo.title: Agentic AI in Finance: What Kraft Heinz Teaches
seo.description: Kraft Heinz booked $208 million in improper savings. See what it reveals about agentic AI in finance and what to fix before you automate.

title: What does Kraft Heinz's $208 million fraud say about agentic AI in finance?
excerpt: Kraft Heinz booked $208 million in improper savings and nobody checked where they came from. Before automating finance with agentic AI, see what needs an owner.

content.content: Kraft Heinz: why agentic AI only works with process governance

In 2017, Kraft Heinz, an American multinational food company (kraftheinzcompany.com), needed its EBITDA to grow 6.1% for its teams to receive bonuses. EBITDA is operating profit before interest, taxes and depreciation. The company delivered 3%, less than half the target.

content.title: In this article
content.content: Who benefited from Kraft Heinz's fake discounts, why the number reaches consolidation with no origin, what process governance is, why agentic AI cannot fix this alone and how to prepare before you automate.

Under pressure from the chief operating officer for savings the budget did not support, procurement (the purchasing department) structured supplier contracts so that savings that did not yet exist could be booked. The head of procurement approved the contracts. Controllership, the function that closes the company's numbers, added up what it received. Later, the restatement corrected $208 million in improper savings, from 295 transactions between 2015 and 2018. The fraud was deliberate. What let it through was a process governance failure: in consolidation, nothing recorded where each number came from.

That is where agentic AI can stall too. Agentic AI means AI systems that carry out tasks on their own, such as adding up and reconciling the numbers in a budget. Talk about it in finance usually centers on automation and productivity. The rush not to fall behind pushes governance into second place. The thesis here is simple: agentic AI does not fix a process without governance, it only speeds it up. To see why, start inside Kraft Heinz.
Who benefited from Kraft Heinz's improper savings?

Incentives explain most of it. The bonus depended on hitting the EBITDA target. The chief operating officer's pressure carried that target down to procurement. Every booked saving moved the result closer to it. Consolidation, the step where every department's numbers are added into the company's results, had no stage that traced where each saving came from. Whoever booked the savings gained. Whoever added the numbers was not paid to doubt them.

3G Capital, the investment firm that controls Kraft Heinz, used zero-based budgeting, in which every expense must be justified from scratch each cycle. The practice is legitimate and it is not the villain of this story. It only raised the pressure on the people who had to show savings.

The bill arrived in stages. In February 2019, the company announced a $15.4 billion write-down of goodwill (the premium paid for acquisitions above the value of their assets) and of brands such as Kraft and Oscar Mayer, with a net loss of $12.6 billion for the quarter. In June 2019, it restated its financial statements, the official earnings reports, correcting $208 million in improper savings. In 2021, it paid a $62 million penalty to the SEC, the US regulator of securities markets. Both executives were also penalized: the chief operating officer paid $300,000, while the chief procurement officer paid $100,000 and was barred for 5 years from serving as an officer or director of a public company. In 2023, the settlement with shareholders cost another $450 million.
Why does the number reach consolidation with no origin?

In consolidation, the number arrives without its origin. Every number has an assumption, the reason to believe it. The number is "$1 million in discounts." The assumption is "the supplier agreed in writing and will deduct it from the invoice." When only the number arrives, the person adding things up sees just the total. At Kraft Heinz, what reached controllership was a contract that described the discount differently. Nobody checked the assumption behind it.

There was bad faith on the part of those who built the contracts. Even so, the lesson lies in the process, which had no way to notice. A simple question was missing, one that should be asked at every step: where did this number come from? Who confirms the assumption behind it? With nobody owning that question, the approval chain gets long, the pressure to hit targets stays real and visibility into the number's origin shrinks.

Silent error is more common than deliberate fraud. In most companies nobody is trying to fool anybody. There is simply a number everyone uses and nobody can explain. Kraft Heinz is the extreme case of the same weakness.
The problem is process governance

Process governance is the set of rules that records, for every number in the budget, who booked it, on what basis and who checked it before it was added to the result. At Kraft Heinz, that governance did not exist in consolidation. With agentic AI the problem is the same, because AI also books and changes numbers. What changes is who books them and how fast.

content.content: Why can't agentic AI in finance fix this on its own?

A 2025 survey, cited by Neurons Lab, an agentic AI engineering consultancy (neurons-lab.com), found that 99% of companies plan to put AI agents into production in finance. Only 11% have done so. The most cited reason is not the price of the technology. It is data, governance and security, the foundation any agent works on.

Intuition says the tools are missing. The data says the foundation is missing. An AI agent runs rules on whatever already exists, whether that is a process with governance or one without. If the budget runs without version control and without a record of who approved each number, the agent adds everything up with the same confidence, including the saving that did not yet exist. In January 2026, Lloyds Banking Group, a British bank (lloydsbankinggroup.com), called 2026 the year agentic AI moves from experimentation to use at scale. The same bank says it deploys its agents with rigorous testing, human oversight and real-time monitoring.

Now picture what that would have done at Kraft Heinz. The scheme took three years to surface because nobody traced where each saving came from. An agent that consolidates in minutes, without that tracing, would have grown the same pattern to the same size in months.

A lack of process governance already has a price. At Kraft Heinz it was $208 million corrected in earnings, a $62 million penalty and a $450 million shareholder settlement, all because nobody in consolidation checked where each saving came from. When every number has an owner and a record, the error surfaces at its source, before consolidation. Without tracing, it surfaces years later, on an auditor's bill.
How to apply this before automating
Process governance starts with three written answers for every number in the budget or the close: who booked it, on what basis and who checked it before it entered consolidation.

Start with the points in the current process where a number changes hands without a record of who approved it, especially where targets create pressure, as they did in Kraft Heinz's procurement department, pushed by the chief operating officer. Those are the points where AI, if it arrives before governance, will amplify the problem. One point of the process at a time is enough to start.

The three answers sit with controllership, the function responsible for the reliability of the company's numbers. It differs from auditing, which finds the problem after it has happened, as it did at Kraft Heinz, when the bill already ran into the billions.
How the question changes
The usual question is when the company will be able to use agentic AI in finance. The better question is which number in today's budget nobody could explain. Kraft Heinz answered it without any AI.

AI does not create the process governance problem. It shortens the time the problem takes to appear. So a company that organizes the origin of its numbers before automating decides whether AI will work for its results or against them.
